grammar.title: The Sentence
grammar.html:
You have learnt that a sentence is a group of words that makes complete sense. A sentence always has at least one finite verb. A sentence starts with a capital letter and ends with a full stop, a question mark or an exclamation mark.

Subject and Predicate
A sentence consists of two parts—the subject and the predicate.

In a sentence, the subject may be the person or thing that does the action or the one on whom the action is performed. For example,
- The swimmer dived into the pool.
- The spacecraft was launched.

In the first sentence, the subject is the swimmer who does the action; and in the second sentence, the action is performed on the subject, that is, the spacecraft. The rest of the sentence, excluding the subject, is known as the predicate.

NOTE:
A finite verb is a verb that shows the person and number of the subject. For example,
- Birds fly south for the winter.
- Ravi's parrot flies in and out of its cage.

NOTE:
To identify the subject of the sentence, we usually ask the question who or what before the verb. In the given examples, we can identify the subject by asking—
- Who dived into the pool?
- What was launched?

The subject of the sentence is the part which denotes the person or the thing we are talking about.

The predicate is that part of the sentence which tells us about the subject. The predicate will always include the verb.

The subject usually comes at the beginning of a sentence and is followed by the predicate. However, there are exceptions.
- In lines of poetry, the subject might come after the predicate.
- Out of the sea came he!
- In questions, the subject comes after the helping verb.
- Can I be of any help?
- In imperative sentences, the subject is often implied or understood.
- (You) Go home as soon as you finish this work.

The subject of a sentence may be one or several words. The word that is most important in such a phrase is then called the subject-word. Look at these sentences where the subjects have been highlighted and the subject-word underlined in each case.

  • The weather was hot.
  • The hot weather caused the death of many birds.
  • The weather, being sultry, spoilt our picnic plans.

In the second and third sentences above, the subject-words have been qualified by an adjective (hot) and a group of words that acts as an adjective (being sultry), respectively. The is also considered to be an attribute.

NOTE:
The subject-word is always a noun, or a group of words that acts as a noun. For example,
- To err is human. (infinitive acting as noun)
- Walking is excellent exercise. (gerund acting as noun)

The adjective or the adjective phrase that qualifies the subject-word in a sentence is called the attribute.

A. Look at these excerpts from some famous poems. Identify the subject and the subject-word as well as its attribute in each sentence. Underline the predicates. Put a (/) where the subject has been omitted.

  1. A crumb of cake would be a feast
    And last you seven days at least.
    A flea would be a frightening beast.
    If you were one inch tall. (Shel Silverstein)
  2. Out of the huts of history's shame
    I rise.
    Up from a past that's rooted in pain
    I rise. (Maya Angelou)
  3. Do not go gentle into that good night.
    Old age should burn and rave at close of day.
    Rage, rage against the dying of the light.
    (Dylan Thomas)
  4. Where now is the horse and the rider?
    Where is the horn that was blowing?
    (J R R Tolkien)

Like the subject, the predicate of a sentence is usually made up of more than one word.

Sometimes, the verb in a sentence may be qualified by an adverb or a group of words that works as an adverb. Look at these sentences where the verb has been underlined and the qualifying word or group of words has been highlighted.
- Ravi runs fast.
- We ran all the way.

An adverb or an adverb phrase that qualifies the verb is called the adverbial qualification.

NOTE:
If the predicate of a sentence is only one word, that word will be a verb.
For example,
- Lions roar.
- A penguin brays.

You have learnt that a verb in a sentence may be used transitively or intransitively. When the verb is used transitively, it may take one or more objects.

NOTE:
When a verb requires an object to receive its action, we say the verb is used transitively. A verb whose meaning is complete without an object is said to be used intransitively. For example,
- The little dog is chasing a rat. (transitive)
- The rat is running away as fast as possible. (intransitive)

The person or thing that receives the action of the verb is called the object of the verb.

Look at these sentences.
- Sarita is reading a book.
- I love peanut butter sandwiches.
- Tara met her childhood friends after ages.
In the above sentences, the verb has only one object—the direct object, which we identify by asking the question who/what after the verb.

Now, read these sentences.
- Manisha is making tea for her guests.
- Akshay gave a beautiful pendant to his mother.
- The children received a letter from their father.
In the above sentences, the verbs take two objects—direct and indirect. The indirect object is identified by asking the question to/for/from + whom/what after the verb.

Intransitive verbs do not have objects, but sometimes they require a word or a group of words to complete their sense. Look at these examples.
- Mira is a doctor.
- Romit seems to be a studious boy.
The highlighted words in the above sentences are required to make the sentences complete and meaningful. They tell us something more about the subjects of the verbs.

A word or a group of words that is required to complete the sense of a verb, and that tells us something about the subject of the verb is called the subjective complement.

Now, read these sentences. Note that in the absence of the highlighted words, the sentences would sound incomplete.
- I appointed him captain.
- They proved me wrong.
Here, the words captain and wrong tell us something about the object of the verbs, namely him and me.

A word or a group of words that is required to complete the sense of the predicate and that tells us more about the object of the verb is called the objective complement.

20. The king, dressed in regal splendour, walked to the temple.

Kinds of Sentences
You have learnt that a sentence can be a statement, a question, a request, a command, a denial or a response.

Read these sentences.
- I like mangoes.
- It is not raining.
- Our pet dog is very playful.
All these sentences state something.

An assertive sentence makes a statement. It is also known as a declarative sentence.

NOTE:
An assertive sentence begins with a capital letter and ends with a full stop (.).

Assertive sentences are of two kinds—affirmative and negative sentences. Look at these sentences.
- The knife is blunt.
- The knife is not sharp.
The two sentences convey the same meaning, but one does so negatively, while the other states it positively.

A sentence that tells us that something exists or something is happening is called an affirmative sentence. An affirmative sentence is also known as a positive sentence.

A sentence that states that something does not exist or that something is not happening is called a negative sentence.

NOTE:
Negative sentences usually contain not or no.

Read these sentences that ask questions.
- Where is my umbrella?
- Has the gardener sown the seeds?

An interrogative sentence asks questions.

There are two kinds of interrogative sentences—yes or no questions and wh- questions.

Read these sentences.
- Can you swim?
- Does your brother play tennis?

NOTE:
An interrogative sentence always ends with a question mark (?).

When we ask these questions, we expect the answer to be yes or no, so they are called yes or no questions.

We use helping verbs like be, have, do, can, should, may or will to ask yes or no questions. In such questions, the helping verb comes before the subject and the main verb comes after the subject.

For example,
- Can you read out this story?
- Are the Guptas coming?

Now, read these sentences.
- Where did you go yesterday?
- What have you done to my phone?

Questions that begin with why, what, when, which, who, where, whom and how are called wh- questions.

Like yes or no questions, in wh- questions too, the helping verb comes before the subject and the main verb comes after the subject.

NOTE:
Sometimes, what, who or which may act as the subject of the sentence. For example,
- Who committed this mistake?
- Who left the lights on?

Now, read these sentences.
- Go away. (order)
- Please close the window. (request)
- Study well. (advice)

A sentence that gives a command or an order, makes a request or gives advice is called an imperative sentence.

In an imperative sentence, the subject is usually left out. The subject is understood to be you in most sentences. For example,
- (You) Apologise right now.
- (You) Go away.

Now, read these sentences.
- What a lovely painting!
- What a miss!

A sentence that expresses strong feeling is called an exclamatory sentence.

NOTE:
Not all imperative sentences are necessarily commands. They can be social expressions. For example,
- Get well soon.
- Have a nice day.

NOTE:
An exclamatory sentence always ends with an exclamation mark (!).

C. Rearrange the words and phrases to form meaningful sentences as directed in the brackets.
1. young/ worried / the / man / how/ looks (exclamatory)
2. how many / are there / do you know / in our lives / sources of stress (interrogative)
3. are four / of stress / sources / our lives / there / in / common (assertive)

7. of / is / another / anxiety / source / stress (assertive)
8. panic / goes wrong / when / do not / any little thing (imperative)

Transformation of Sentences
You have learnt that it is possible to change the form of a sentence without entirely changing the meaning. Look at these pairs of sentences that convey the same meaning.
- How sweet the song is! (exclamatory)
- The song is very sweet. (assertive)
- Aren't elephants very intelligent? (interrogative)
- Elephants are very intelligent. (assertive)
- He did the work. (affirmative)
- He did not fail to do the work. (negative)

D. Change these sentences as directed.

2. What a curt reply! (to assertive)
3. I will not reach early. (to affirmative)
4. No man is immortal. (to interrogative)

6. Who does not know this? (to assertive)

10. You should not break rules. (to imperative)
11. I wish I had come sooner. (to exclamatory)

13. That was not the correct thing to say. (to interrogative)
14. As soon as he saw the policeman, he ran. (to negative)
15. Was it for this that we worked so hard? (to assertive)
16. You are instructed to sit down immediately. (to imperative)
17. There was no one present who did not reply. (to affirmative)
18. In the opposition too, the orthodox fought against the bill. (to negative)
19. Was there ever anything so exquisitely beautiful before? (to assertive)
20. I shall never forget those glorious days in school. (to interrogative)
21. You must solve all the sums in this exercise before turning on the television. (to negative)
22. You must not run or shout in the corridor. (to imperative)
23. This carpet is an exquisite work of art. (to exclamatory)
24. Who thought it would rain so heavily today? (to assertive)
25. The minister whispered in the emperor's ear. (to interrogative)

grammar.title: Modals
grammar.html:
Read this conversation. Observe the function of the highlighted words.

Rakhi: May I come in, ma'am?
Teacher: You must not be late for class.
Rakhi: I'm sorry, ma'am. I had to meet the maths teacher, but I could not find her, so I got late. It will not happen again.
Teacher: Very well. But you ought to excuse yourself first.

The highlighted words above are verbs that are tell us more about the mood or the attitude of the speaker. You have learnt that such words are called modals.

Modals, or modal auxiliaries, are verbs that are used to express the mood or attitude of the speaker.

NOTE:
You have learnt that auxiliaries, or helping verbs, are of two kinds—primary auxiliaries and modal auxiliaries. The primary auxiliaries are the verbs be, have and do when they are used with other verbs. Look at this table that lists the forms and functions of these verbs.

Forms Functions Examples
be (present—is, am, are; past—was, were) form continuous tenses, used in the passive and to denote a command or a plan - I am writing a letter. - The door was opened by Shyam. - You are to leave right now.
have (present—has, have; past—had) form the perfect tenses - I have completed my work. - Ma had made orange pudding.
do (present—does, do; past—did) form interrogatives, imperatives and negative sentences - Do you know that girl? - Do be patient. - He doesn't agree.

The verbs be, have and do can also be used as principal, or main verbs. For example,
- I am a student. (reveals a state of being)
- I have a pet dog. (indicates ownership)
- I do yoga every day. (shows action)

The most commonly used modals are can, could, may, might, shall, should, must, will, would, used, need, dare and ought. These are used to express possibility, certainty, necessity, ability, expectation, permission, advice, wish or obligation. Let us now study the use of modal auxiliaries in detail.

NOTE:
Modals are always followed by a main verb. They do not change form with the person or the number of the subject.

Can is used—
- to talk about ability and possibility. For example,
- She can play tennis very well. (ability)
- Loud noise can damage your ears. (possibility)
- to ask for and give permission in an informal manner. For example,
- Can I join the gym from tomorrow? (seeking permission)
- You can meet me tomorrow. (giving permission)
Could is used—
- as the past equivalent of can in indirect speech. For example,
- Mani said, 'I can help you.'
- Mani said that she could help me.
- to make polite requests. For example,
- Could you help me carry these bags?
- to indicate ability in the past. For example,
- She could do handstands once upon a time.
May is used—
- to ask for permission in a formal manner. For example,
- May I come in, sir?
- to express a wish. For example,
- May you always enjoy good luck!
- to indicate a weak possibility. For example,
- It may rain this afternoon.
Might is used—
- to suggest a very weak possibility in the future. For example,
- It might rain tonight.
- Don't play with the knives. You might get hurt.
- as the past equivalent of may in indirect speech. For example,
- Jiya said, 'I may get the job.'
- Jiya said that she might get the job.
Will is used—
- to talk about future events that are planned or about which we are certain. For example,
- The train will leave at 10 a.m.
- My mother will turn sixty this year.
- to show determination or willingness. For example,
- I will help you complete the assignment.
- to make polite requests. For example,
- Will you help me complete the assignment?
- Will you turn down the music, please? I am trying to sleep.
Shall is used—
- to make offers or suggestions. For example,
- Shall I close the door?
- to show certainty or promise. For example,
- I shall clean the kitchen tomorrow.
- in the second and third person to express a command, a promise or even a threat. For example,
- He shall not come here again. (threat)
- You shall certainly receive a raise. (promise)

Would is used—
- to make polite requests. For example,
- Would you mind lending me your pen?
- to talk about past habits. For example,
- After dinner, we would sit and talk for hours.

NOTE:
Shall is usually used with the first person singular (I) or the first person plural (we).
- to talk about imaginary situations. For example,
- I would love to go to Morocco.

Should is used—
- to express advice, suggestion or obligation. For example,
- You should tell the truth.
- to express probability. For example,
- You should find this grammar book helpful.
Must is used—
- to express necessity or obligation. For example,
- We must do this right away.
- to give advice to someone, especially when we want to emphasis that it is for their own good. For example,
- You must stop lying.
Ought to is used—
- to express duty or moral obligation. For example,
- We ought to obey our parents. (duty)
- We ought to protect our national monuments. (moral obligation)
- to express necessity. For example,
- We ought to buy a cupboard.
Used is used—
- to indicate something that was a habit, but has been discontinued. For example,
- She used to learn yoga.
Need is used—
- to denote necessity or obligation. For example,
- Jaya need not go to the post office.
- Do I need to help him?

NOTE:
As an ordinary verb, need means want or require. For example,
- I do not need your help.

Dare is used—
- in interrogative and negative sentences where the implication is to be bold enough to.
- How dare you say so?
- to imply a challenge. For example,
- I dare you to finish up the whole pizza.

NOTE:
Notice how the use of modals affects the meaning of a sentence.
- You must do it. (means it is necessary that you do it)
- You mustn't do it. (means it is necessary that you do not do it)
- You needn't do it. (means it is not necessary for you to do it)
- You ought to do it. (expresses moral obligation or desirability)

grammar.title: Nouns
grammar.html:
A noun is the name of a person, a place, an animal, a feeling or an idea.

Kinds of Noun
Nouns can be classified into five kinds.

The name of a particular person, place, monument or building is called a proper noun. For example, Florence Nightingale, Mumbai, Howrah Bridge.

NOTE:
Proper nouns always begin with a capital letter. We do not use a, an or the before proper nouns.

The name of a person, place, or building in general is called a common noun. For example, man, river, monument.

The name used for a collection of people, animals, birds or objects is called a collective noun. For example, flock, herd, family.

The name of an idea, a concept, a state of being or a feeling is called an abstract noun. For example, beauty, hatred, trust.

The name of the matter or substance of which a thing is made is called a material noun. For example, silver, wood, paper.

grammar.title: Non-Finite Verbs
grammar.html:
You have learnt that verbs can be finite or non-finite.

A verb that has a subject and shows tense, person and number is called a finite verb.

For example,
- I live in New Delhi.
- My sister lives in Mumbai.

A verb that has no subject, and does not show person or number is called a non-finite verb.

For example,
- I love to go to the mall.
- Reena sat waiting quietly.

There are three kinds of non-finite verbs—infinitives, participles and gerunds. Let us learn about them in detail.

Infinitives
Read these sentences.
- I want to sing.
- She wants to improve her English.
In these sentences, the verb want is the finite verb. To sing and to improve are the infinitives.

Infinitives are also called the to-verb because to is often used to form an infinitive. Let us look at the functions of the infinitive.

An infinitive can be used—
- as the subject of the verb in a sentence. For example,
- To lie is bad.
- as the object of the verb in a sentence. For example,
- I want to dance.
- as the subject of the verb, but it also takes an object of its own. For example,
- To respect our parents is our duty.
- as the object of the verb but it also takes an object of its own. For example,
- I expect to complete the task.
- as the object of the verb and also be modified by an adverb. For example,
- Many of the singers preferred to sing softly.
- to qualify an adjective or a noun. For example,
- This is not the time to laze.
- Quinine is bitter to taste.
- as the object of a preposition. For example,
- The concert is about to end.
- as the complement of a verb. For example,
- This is to ensure your safety.

NOTE:
Infinitives are useful when—
- we wish to state an aim or purpose.
- He called to thank me.
- He wanted to borrow some money.
- They agreed to consider our case.
- we wish to indicate result.
- My great-grandmother lived to see me succeed.

We usually use to with the infinitive. However, it is not essential. Look at these instances where we do not use to.

We do not use to with the infinitive—

  • with modals. For example,
  • The child may go.
  • after verbs of perception like see, hear, watch, know and feel. For example,
    • I saw the clouds gather in the sky.
  • after verbs like make and let. For example,
    • Paula made him cry.
    • Let me do this now.
  • after the conjunction but.
    For example,
  • The child did nothing but sleep.
  • after had better, had rather, sooner than, etc. For example,
    • She had better leave now.

NOTE:
With verbs like need and dare, we use the infinitive with to in affirmative sentences, but not in interrogatives or negative sentences. For example,
- How dare you create such a ruckus?
- Rina dared her sister to do this reckless act.
- I need not finish the work yet.
- I need to find a good plumber soon.

Participles

Read these sentences.

The highlighted words are present participles that have been used as verbs and as adjectives connected to the underlined noun and pronoun.

Present participle forms of verbs always end in -ing. Such words represent actions that are going on, or are incomplete.

Now, look at these sentences.
- Duped by our tour guide, we returned to the hotel.
- We saw a few women bent by the weight of heavy sacks.
The highlighted words are examples of past participles that have been used as verbs and as adjectives modifying the underlined pronoun and noun, respectively.

Past participle forms of verbs usually end in -ed/-t/-n. They describe actions that have been completed.

NOTE:
Look at this sentence.
- Walking down the road, amusing sight was seen.
In this sentence, there is no noun or pronoun to which the participle walking refers.
The sentence should be written as—
- Walking down the road, I saw an amusing sight.

Now, read these sentences.
- The piercing scream broke the silence.
- The barking dogs ran around.

The participles in the above sentences have been used simply as qualifying adjectives. They are known as participial adjectives.

NOTE:
We may say that a participle is a verbal adjective.

Participles may be used—
- as attributes. For example,
- The broken glass lay scattered on the ground.
- A lost chance never returns.
- in the predicate, modifying the subject or the object. For example,
- We found the child weeping.
- He kept us waiting.
- as a subjective complement. For example,
- The story was interesting.
- The trek was very tiring.
- as part of a phrase that functions as an adjective. For example,
- The boy standing at the gate is my brother.

We can join pairs of sentences by using participles. For example,
- The boy saw a dog. It was coming towards him.
- The boy saw a dog coming towards him.
- Sheila opened the box. She took out an old manuscript.
- Opening the cupboard, Sheila took out an old manuscript.

In the above examples, both actions take place at the same time. When we join the sentences, one finite verb is removed. So we use the continuous form of the participle.

But sometimes, the second action begins only after the first has been completed. In that case, we convert the verb denoting the first action into a participle. For example,
- He had lost all his money. He went to his mother for help.
- Having lost all his money, he went to his mother for help.
This is an example of perfect participle where the action has been completed at some point of time in the past.

In these sentences, the -ing words function like nouns. However, all these words are derived from verbs.

When the -ing form of the verb is used as a noun in a sentence, we call it the gerund.

NOTE:
The -ing word can be used in different ways. For example,
- Collecting stamps is her hobby. (subject)
- I don't like writing. (object)
- My favourite hobby is reading. (complement of the sentence)

Gerunds or Infinitives?
As both gerunds and infinitives have the force of a noun and a verb, they have the same uses. Thus, in many sentences either of them may be used. For example,
- He likes singing. (gerund)
- He likes to sing. (infinitive)
- She began laughing. (gerund)
- She began to laugh. (infinitive)

However, the only non-finite form of the verb that can follow a preposition is a gerund. For example,
- They were punished for to lie. (infinitive, incorrect)
- They were punished for lying. (gerund, correct)
- We cannot live without to drink water. (infinitive, incorrect)
- We cannot live without drinking water. (gerund, correct)

grammar.html:
Read these sentences. Can you say why they sound funny?
- This is pen.
- I just had sandwich.

The above sentences have been rewritten correctly. Underline the words that have been added to complete the sentences.
- This is my pen.
- I just had a sandwich.
- The boy in the red shirt is my brother.
- The mangoes in this basket are sweet.

The words you have just underlined come before nouns and help to identify or specify which person or thing is being referred to. These words are called determiners.

Determiners are used before nouns to indicate which particular person or thing we are referring to. They do not describe nouns, but point them out.

There are six different kinds of determiners.
- articles
- possessives
- quantifiers
- demonstratives
- interrogatives
- distributes

Articles
You have learnt that there are three articles—a, an and the.

The words a and an are called indefinite articles because they do not point to any special person or thing.

The word the is known as the definite article because it points to a specific person or thing.

The definite article is used—
- to make a specific reference. For example,
- There's the shop I was looking for.
- when we are talking to someone who knows which thing or person we are referring to. For example,
- There is water in the fridge.
- Turn the television on.
- to generalise a class
- The tiger is an endangered species.
- before an adjective, when it is used as a noun indicating nationality or a class. For example,
- The rich can be selfish.
- The Swiss are famous for their watches and chocolates.
- before the names of rivers, seas, oceans or mountains. For example, the Alps, the Indian Ocean.
- before the names of parts of the body when these are referred to in an impersonal way. For example,
- He was hit on the head.

The indefinite articles are used with singular countable nouns. The article a is used before words starting with a consonant sound while an is used before words beginning with a vowel sound. The indefinite articles are also used—
- to refer to something mentioned for the first time. For example,
- I bought a newspaper at the station.
- It was an interesting idea.
- to refer to something you do not want to be specific about. For example,
- A girl came to see you.
- to refer to a person's profession. For example,
- He is an engineer.
- in definitions. For example,
- An opossum is a marsupial.

NOTE:
If there is an adjective before a singular countable noun, we place the article in front of the adjective. For example,
- a monthly magazine
- an African elephant
- a united country
- an honourable task
Note that we use an before honourable since it begins with a vowel sound (o), while united begins with a consonant sound (you) and is thus preceded by a.

It is important to remember that we do not use articles—
- with uncountable nouns. For example,
- I always welcome good news.
- with plural nouns. For example,
- Teachers enjoy long vacations.
- with the names of holidays. For example,
- I will meet my uncle during Easter.
- with the names of months. For example,
- Last September, he was in London.
- with the names of the days of the week. For example,
- We will go out on Sunday.
- with the names of seasons. For example,
- Siberian cranes visit the sanctuary in winter.
- when we speak of the time of the day or with the names of meals. For example,
- I should finish by noon.
- What shall we have for dinner?
- with words such as 'hospital' 'university' or 'school', when they are used for their intended purpose, that is, medical, educational, etc. For example,
- He'll have to stay in hospital for a while.

NOTE:
- We use the with a plural or uncountable noun, when we are talking of something specific. For example,
- Flowers make a room look bright.
- The flowers were delivered this morning.
- We use the if we know which season we are referring to. For example,
- In the summer of 1999, we were all down with measles.
- We use a, an or the when we refer to the time of a particular day. For example,
- When I woke up in the morning, I saw grey clouds.
- We use articles when we refer to them as a particular place or buildings. For example,
- I went to the hospital yesterday to see my aunt.

I left place eager to learn. Everything had name, and each name gave birth to new thought. As we returned to house, every object I touched seemed to quiver with life. I entered house. I remembered broken doll. It was gift from Miss Sullivan. I felt my way to hearth and picked up pieces. My eyes filled with tears. I was filled with sense of regret. Incident proved to be turning point in my life. Not only had I learnt importance of words, I had also understood what nice teacher I had. I had been given opportunity to explore wide world of language. Children who hear acquire language without any particular effort. Deaf child is at disadvantage. The process of learning language is slow one. The deaf child does not learn in month. It was long time before I had something appropriate to say at right time.

Demonstratives
Let us revise what you have learnt about the use of the four demonstratives—this, that, these and those.

Demonstrative determiners help to point to specific nouns.

We use this and these to refer to people or objects that are nearby while that and those are used in the context of people or objects that are at a distance. For example,
- This book is heavier than that one.
- These mangoes are sweeter than those ones.

As you can see in the above sentences, we use this and that before singular nouns while these and those are used before plural nouns.

NOTE:
We can use this and that before uncountable nouns as well as countable nouns. For example,
- Who has spilled this milk?
- That apple is rotten.

Possessives
Read these sentences.
- I gave my sandwich to his brother.
- Put my book in her bag.

The highlighted adjectives show possession or belonging and are possessive determiners.

The possessive determiners are my, our, your, his, her, its and their. These can be used before singular and plural nouns regardless of whether they are countable or uncountable.

Interrogatives
Read these sentences.
- Which sari should I buy?
- What book are they reading?

The highlighted adjectives are used in interrogative sentences to gather information about the noun in question and are called interrogative determiners.

The words what, which, whose, how much and how many are interrogatives and they can be used before any noun.

Quantifiers
Read these sentences.
- Can you lend me some sugar?
- Few people turned up for the meeting.

The highlighted words provide information about the quantity of a noun and are called quantifiers.

Some common quantifiers are any, much, many, several, little, some and few. These can be used to suggest number as well as quantity and are accordingly used with countable or uncountable nouns.

We use many, several and few with plural countable nouns since they suggest number. For example, many lions, several bushes.

The quantifiers much and little refer to quantity and can only be used before uncountable nouns. For example, much work, little hope.

The words some and any can be used before countable as well as uncountable nouns. However, we generally use some in affirmative sentences and any in negative sentences.
- Some houses are being renovated in that area.
- I don't have any money to spare at the moment.

Distributives
Read these sentences.
- Neither boy deserves this award.
- You can take either road to reach his house.
- Every student must attend assembly.
- She has solved each sample paper at least twice.

The highlighted words point out that the people or things mentioned are to be considered separately and are thus called distributives.

NOTE:
We also use any when we wish to suggest that we are not looking for something specific. For example,
- We can watch any movie that you like.

grammar.title: Perfect and Perfect Continuous Tenses
grammar.html:
You have learnt that the perfect tenses show that an action has already been completed. The word perfect implies completed. Let us revise what you have learnt about the perfect tenses.

Present Perfect Tense
Both the simple past tense and the present perfect tense express an action completed in the past. The simple past tense expresses an action completed in the past but not linked to the present. The present perfect tense, however, denotes an action that is completed but connected to the present. The present perfect tense is used—

  • to indicate an action that has been completed just now or a little while ago. For example,
    • They have bought a car.
    • I have called for a cab.
  • to express an action whose time is not given and is not definite. For example,
    • He has lived in Bangkok.
  • to describe a past event which has its effect on the present. For example,
    • I have lost the keys to the house. (So I cannot open the door.)
  • to talk about a continuing state, not action. For example,
    • Girish has been ill since Monday.
    • Mini has broken her leg.
    • We have known the Guptas for twenty years.

NOTE:
We use since to talk about a point of time in the past like Tuesday, 9 o'clock. We use for to talk about a period or duration of time like two weeks, five years.

Past Perfect Tense
The past perfect tense is used to denote an action that took place before another action. For example,
- When I reached the bus stop, the bus had left.

The tenses of the verbs in this sentence show which action happened first. The past perfect (had left) is used for the earlier action and the simple past (reached) for the later action.

The past perfect tense is also used to indicate a past hope or desire that has remained unfulfilled. We use verbs like hope, expect, think in such cases. For example,
- I had expected to win the tournament.

Future Perfect Tense
The future perfect tense is used to refer to the completion of an action by a certain time in the future. The tense is normally used with expressions like by that time, by then, by next week. For example,
- I will have completed the assignment by next week.
- The coach will have arrived by 11:00 a.m.

Present Perfect Continuous Tense

The present perfect continuous is used—
- to denote an action that began at some time in the past and is still continuing. For example,
- I have been swimming for two hours.
- Kate has been working since six in the morning.
- to denote repeated actions. For example,
- I have been getting this journal every week for a year.

NOTE:
There is sometimes very little difference between the meaning of the present perfect and the meaning of the present perfect continuous tense.
- I have been working at this site for three years.
- I have worked here for three years.

Past Perfect Continuous Tense
The past perfect continuous is used—
- to denote that an action that began before a particular moment in the past and was still taking place, or had just finished, at that moment when another action took place. For example,
- When I visited Gwalior, he had been teaching there for a year.
- I had been driving for an hour when I heard a sound in the gear box.
- to talk about repeated actions in the past. For example,
- She had been trying to fix this all day.

Future Perfect Continuous Tense
The future perfect continuous is used—
- to indicate an action has been in progress over a period of time and will end in the future. For example,
- By the end of the year, I shall have been living in Delhi for seven years.
- When their mother returns home at five o'clock, Rita will have been watching television for four hours.

grammar.title: Active and Passive Voice
grammar.html:
Read these sentences.

  • He painted a picture.
  • A picture was painted by him.

Both the sentences have the same meaning but have been constructed differently. In the first sentence, the highlighted verb indicates that the subject (he) did the action. In the second sentence, the function of the verb is to show that the subject (a picture) was acted on.

The verb that expresses that the action is carried out by the subject is said to be in the active voice. The active voice is used when the agent or the doer is to be made prominent.

The verb that expresses what is done to the subject is said to be in the passive voice.

See how the following sentences in the active voice have been changed into passive voice without changing their meanings.
- The referee ordered a re-match.
- A re-match was ordered by the referee.
- Shireen bought a house.
- A house was bought by Shireen.

NOTE:
The last word of any verb in the passive form will be written in the past participle form.

Let us revise the rules of conversion from active to passive voice.
- The positions of the subject and the object of the active verb are interchanged. The subject of the verb in the active voice is made the object of the verb in the passive voice.
- In the passive voice, the preposition by is added before the object.
- The number of the verb is changed according to the number and person of the subject.
- He loves me.
- I am loved by him.
- Active verbs followed by a preposition retain the preposition. For example,
- The students laughed at the clown.
- The clown was laughed at by the students.

Not all tenses take the passive form. Study the table to understand how the verb is changed into the passive voice form in different tenses.

Tense Active voice Passive voice
Simple present He reads a book. A book is read by him.
Present continuous He is reading a book. A book is being read by him.
Present perfect He has read a book. A book has been read by him.
Present perfect continuous He has been reading a book. —
Simple past He read a book. A book was read by him.
Past continuous He was reading a book. A book was being read by him.
Past perfect He had read a book. A book had been read by him.
Past perfect continuous He had been reading a book. —
Simple future He will read a book. A book will be read by him.
Future continuous He will be reading a book. —
Future perfect He will have read a book. A book will have been read by him.
Future perfect continuous He will have been reading a book. —

NOTE:
- If the active verb has two objects—one direct and the other indirect—either of them becomes the subject of the passive verb, and the other remains as an object in the passive voice. The object that comes after the passive verb is called the retained object. For example,
- My father gave me a calculator. (active voice)
- I was given a calculator by my father. (passive voice)
- A calculator was given to me by my father. (passive voice)

    Let + object + be + past participle
  • If the sentence is in the negative, the form is—
    Let not + object + be + past participle

The passive voice is used when the person or thing acted upon is to be made prominent. The passive voice is thus preferred when the active form would involve the use of a vague pronoun or noun (somebody, they, people, anybody) as subject. For example,

  • My purse has been stolen. (Someone has stolen my purse.)

We prefer to use the passive voice when—
- the doer is not known or when it is not intended to name him. For example,
- The player was carried out.
- we wish to focus on the person/thing acted upon rather than the doer or the agent. For example,
- The shop was destroyed by lightning.
- the subject in the active voice is implied from the context. For example,
- He was dropped from the team (by the selectors).

NOTE:
Since the object of a verb in the active voice becomes the subject of the passive form, it means that only transitive verbs can be used in the passive, because an intransitive verb has no object.

grammar.title: Transitive and Intransitive Verbs
grammar.html:
We know that there can be no sentences without verbs. A verb tells us—
- what a person or thing does—She designs clothes.
- what is done to a person—The girl was scolded by her mother.
- what a person or thing is—The tiger is a magnificent animal.

A verb can consist of more than one word. For example,
- The boys are playing hockey.
- The actors were rehearsing a play.

Now, look at this sentence.
- My mother polished the vase.
In this sentence, the vase receives the action of the verb.

The person or thing that receives the action of the verb is called the object.

When a verb has an object that receives the action of the verb, it is called the transitive verb.

Now, read this sentence.
- The child cried aloud.
In this sentence, there is no object. The action stops at the doer. No one receives the action of the verb.

When a verb has no object, it is called the intransitive verb.

Most transitive verbs take a single object. But some transitive verbs like give, ask, promise, tell, etc., take two objects—a direct object and an indirect object. For example,
- My father gave me a cycle.

The direct object of the verb is cycle and the indirect object is me.

The person or thing that receives the action of the verb is called the direct object.

The person or thing to whom or on whom the action of the verb is done or who receives the direct object is called the indirect object.

NOTE:
- The direct object of the verb can be identified by asking the question who/what after the verb. The indirect object is identified by asking the question to/for/from + whom/what after the verb. For example,
- The students gave the teacher (indirect) a bouquet of flowers (direct).
- Sometimes, the subject and the object refer to the same person or thing. We then say that the verb has been used reflexively. For example,
- The man hurt himself.
- Do remember that most verbs can be used both transitively as well as intransitively. For example,
- The lions fought the elephants.
- The soldiers fought bravely.
- Some verbs like come, go, fall, die, sleep can never be used transitively.

Verbs of Incomplete Predication

Read these sentences.

  • A dog barks.
  • People laugh.
  • Jackals howl.

These sentences make complete sense. We do not need more words to complete the sense of the verbs.

Now, read these groups of words.

  • The boy appears.
  • She is.
  • She seems.
  • The child continued.

None of these groups of words make sense. We have to add more words to complete the sense of the verbs.

Read these sentences now.

  • The boy appears cheerful.
  • She is focussed.
  • She seems sad.
  • The child continued jumping.

Thus, we see that sometimes, intransitive verbs require more words to make complete sense, and to complete the predicate. Such verbs are called verbs of incomplete predication. The word or words required to make the sense complete is called the complement of the verb.

In the above examples, the underlined complements tell us something about the subject. So these are called subjective complements.

We know that transitive verbs have objects. However, sometimes just an object is not good enough. Read this sentence.
- The members elected Gagan.

We need something more to complete the predicate. For example,
- The members elected Gagan secretary.
Here, the word secretary is referring to Gagan, the object of the verb. So secretary is the objective complement.

grammar.title: Adjectives
grammar.html:
You have learnt that an adjective is a word used to qualify or describe a noun or a pronoun.

Can you say which of the highlighted words below have been used as adjectives? Try to identify the different types of adjectives used.
Kolkata is my city. Kolkata is a big city. It stands on the left bank of the beautiful river Hooghly. This river is a tributary of the Ganges. The river usually has enough water throughout the year. Kolkata has two railway stations. There are many monuments in the city. Each monument is quite stunning. Which monument is my favourite? The Victoria Memorial, of course!

All the highlighted words above have been used to describe or qualify nouns. Let us revise what you have learnt about the different kinds of adjectives.

Adjectives of quality describe the kind or quality of a person or thing. For example, big city, beautiful river.

Adjectives of quantity indicate how much of a thing is meant. For example, little rain, enough water.

Adjectives of number indicate how many of a thing is meant. For example, two stations, six fairies.

NOTE:
Adjectives of number are of three kinds.
- Definite numeral adjectives state the exact number of people or things. They are of two kinds.
- Cardinals tell us the number of people or things. For example, thirty years, twelve days.
- Ordinals tell us the order of people or things in a series. For example, second example, sixth month of the year.
- Indefinite numeral adjectives do not indicate an exact number. For example, few children, many people.
- Distributive numeral adjectives refer to each one of a number. For example, every child, each person.

Demonstrative adjectives indicate which person or thing is meant. For example, this river, those girls.

NOTE:
The words this, that, these and those can be used both as adjectives and as pronouns. It is important to distinguish between the two functions. The easiest way to determine the part of speech is to examine whether the word qualifies a noun or points to a noun. Demonstrative adjectives will always be followed by a noun. For example,
- This is a charming old city. (pronoun, pointing to the noun, city)
- This book is very interesting. (adjective, qualifying the noun, book)

Interrogative adjectives are used with nouns to ask questions. For example which city, whose pen.

Possessive adjectives show belonging or possession. For example, my city, their house.

NOTE:
It is important to understand the difference between possessive adjectives and possessive pronouns. Look at these sentences.
- My aunt wrote me a letter. This aunt of mine lives in Canada.
- Jasbeer spoke to a friend of his about this problem. His friend has promised to help.
